claims.claim: Most of the time, saying less is better.

stances.summary: I have often been sorry for speaking, and never once sorry for keeping quiet. God told me to flee, keep silence and be still.
stances.quote: I have many times repented that I spoke, but that I held my peace I have never repented.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, The Sayings of the Fathers, Book I)
stances.context: Arsenius (d. c. 449), a former tutor at the imperial court who became a hermit at Scetis. The same chapter (saying 2) gives the voice he heard: 'Arsenius, flee, keep silence, and lead a life of silent contemplation, for these are the fundamental causes which prevent a man from committing sin.' Isaac the Syrian (Wensinck translation, Treatise 65) recalls that visitors came to Arsenius and 'he sat with them in silence and dismissed them in silence'. The famous line is older than Arsenius: Plutarch, On Talkativeness 23, credits it to the pagan poet Simonides ('he had often repented of speaking, but never of holding his tongue', https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Moralia/De_garrulitate*.html). Arsenius made it his own, but the reveal should not present it as his invention. The common online wording ('I have often repented of having spoken, but never of having kept silent') is close to Benedicta Ward's 1975 translation, which is copyrighted; use Budge's wording.

stances.summary: He kept a stone in his mouth for three years until he had learned to keep quiet.
stances.quote: They used to say about Abbâ Agathon that for a period of three years he placed a stone in his mouth [and kept it there], until he had learned thoroughly how to hold his peace.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, The Sayings of the Fathers, Book I)
stances.context: Not in the results pool. Fourth-century monk of Scetis. This is a report of his practice by others, not his own words, so it is weaker evidence of a position than a saying. Elsewhere in Budge (ch. 8, saying 356) he quiets his urge to judge others and 'held his peace'.

stances.summary: Asked to give the visiting archbishop a word, he refused: if my silence does not help him, my words will not either.
stances.quote: If by my silence [we] are not helped, [we] shall not be builded by my word.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life)
stances.context: Not in the results pool. Pambo (d. c. 373) of Nitria. The brethren asked him to 'Speak a word to the Bishop' when Theophilus of Alexandria visited Scetis. The same page (saying 196) lists silence as one of his three bodily virtues. Budge's brackets are his own; the Greek has 'he', meaning the archbishop.

stances.summary: His counsel to a monk who asked what to do: do not trust your own goodness, stop dwelling on the past, and keep restraining your tongue and your stomach.
stances.quote: Put no confidence in thine own righteousness, and regret not nor cogitate upon a matter which is past, and be persistent in restraining thy tongue and thy belly.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life)
stances.context: Said to Pambo. The line is one of three counsels, so restraint of speech is part of a wider discipline, not a thesis about silence. Antony was not taciturn with visitors: the Life by Athanasius has him teaching crowds at length. Strength 1 for that reason.

stances.summary: When the other monks insulted him for his colour to test him, he said nothing. He was stung, but he held his tongue.
stances.quote: But Moses hearing this held his peace. And when the congregation was dismissed, they said unto him, “Abbâ Moses, wast thou not afraid?” And he said unto them, “Although I was afraid I uttered not a word.”
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, The Sayings of the Fathers, Book I)
stances.context: The fathers had said 'Why doth this Ethiopian come and go in our midst?' to test him. Same chapter, saying 31: Moses asks the dying Zechariah 'Father, is it good that we should hold our peace?' and is told 'Yea, my son, hold thy peace.' This is silence under insult rather than a general rule about speech, hence strength 1.

stances.summary: Speaking and keeping quiet can both be good, if done for God. A silent man who judges others in his heart is really chattering; a man who talks all day but only says what helps is really silent.
stances.quote: A brother asked Abbâ Poemen, “Which is the better, to speak or to keep silence?” The old man said unto him, “He who speaketh for God’s sake is a good man, and he doeth well, and he who holdeth his peace for God’s sake doeth well.”
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life)
stances.context: Poemen (5th century, Scetis) is the richest voice here because he both prizes silence and refuses to make it a rule. His other sayings in Budge lean toward silence: 'We do not learn to shut a door made of wood, but to close the door of the tongue' (Book I ch. 1, saying 17); 'if thou art asked, speak; and if thou art not asked, hold thy peace' (ch. 1, saying 22); 'say, I am not even worthy to speak' (ch. 1, saying 45). The inward-silence saying is Book I ch. 8, saying 298 (https://www.ecatholic2000.com/athanasius/untitled-195.shtml): 'One man is thought to be silent, yet his heart condemneth others, and he who is thus speaketh everything; and another speaketh from morn until evening, and yet keepeth silence, but such a man speaketh not without profit.' The same saying appears unattributed in ch. 1, saying 27. Overall: mixed, with a lean toward few words.

stances.summary: A learned man who spoke up at a meeting of the desert monks, was told that a stranger should hold his tongue, and accepted it: I spoke once, I will not do it again.
stances.quote: Verily, it is even as thou sayest, O my fathers; I have spoken once, but I will not do it a second time.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, The Sayings of the Fathers, Book I)
stances.context: Heterodox: Evagrius (d. 399) was condemned with Origenism at the council of 553. The story casts him as the talkative scholar who learns silence; saying 58 on the same page has an elder tell him 'speak not before he asketh thee a question', and Evagrius at first bristles: 'Verily I have read many books, and I cannot accept instruction of this kind'. His own treatises also commend stillness, but only modern English translations exist, so they are not quoted here. Strength 1: his position is shown by a story about him, with one line of his own.

stances.summary: Love silence more than anything. At first you force yourself to be quiet, then the silence itself draws you in and gives light that words cannot express.
stances.quote: Love silence above all things. It brings thee near the fruit which the tongue is too weak to interpret. At first we compel ourselves to be silent. Then from our silence something is born which draws us towards silence.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh, 1923
stances.location: Treatise 65 (Wensinck numbering), 'Good advice giving instructions concerning watchfulness', p. 302
stances.context: Isaac (7th century) was a bishop of the Church of the East, a church outside the imperial councils, yet read and venerated by Orthodox and Catholics. He writes for monks living alone. Other lines in the same treatise: 'Every one who possesses profuse speech is certainly empty within, though he tells amazing things' and 'If thou lovest truth, thou must love silence' (p. 300). A later treatise: 'Silence is a symbol of the future world. Speech is an organ of this world.' The popular online wording ('because it brings you near to fruit that the tongue cannot express') is from the 1984 Holy Transfiguration Monastery translation, which is copyrighted; use Wensinck's wording. The djvu text is OCR of the 1923 printing.

stances.summary: Talking a lot is how vanity shows off. The friend of silence comes close to God and is taught by Him in secret.
stances.quote: Much talking is the throne of vainglory, from which it loves to show itself off and parade. [...] The friend of silence draws near to God, and, conversing with Him in secret, is enlightened by God.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (the only complete English translations are modern and copyrighted)
stances.original: Πολυλογία ἐστὶ κενοδοξίας καθέδρα, δι᾿ ἧς ἑαυτὴν ἐμφανίζειν καὶ ἀναπομπεύειν πέφυκε. [...] Ὁ σιωπῆς φίλος προσεγγίζει Θεῷ, καὶ λεληθότως συνομιλῶν φωτίζεται παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ.
stances.context: Climacus (d. c. 649), abbot of Sinai, gives a whole step of the Ladder to this. The step also calls silence joined with knowledge 'mother of prayer' (σιωπὴ ἐν γνώσει μήτηρ προσευχῆς) and ends 'He who has climbed the eleventh step has cut off a host of evils at one stroke.' The step is short and one-sided: no word in favour of talk. The Greek on Wikisource follows the Migne text (PG 88).

stances.summary: A monk should hold his tongue and not speak until spoken to. Even good and holy talk should be rare, because in much speaking you will not escape sin.
stances.quote: The ninth degree of humility is that a monk restrain his tongue from speaking; and, keeping silence, do not speak until he is spoken to.
stances.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages, 1910
stances.original: Nonus humilitatis gradus est, si linguam ad loquendum prohibeat monachus et taciturnitatem habens, usque ad interrogationem non loquatur, monstrante Scriptura quia in multoloquio non effugitur peccatum, et quia vir linguosus non dirigitur super terram.
stances.location: Chapter 7 (the ninth step of humility); see also chapters 4, 6 and 42
stances.context: Written c. 530 for monks in community. Henderson's page omits the text of chapter 6, 'On silence' (De taciturnitate). Its key line, own rendering from the Latin (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/benedict.html): 'So, because of the weight of silence, let permission to speak be seldom granted even to perfect disciples, even for good, holy and edifying talk. For it is written: In much speaking you will not escape sin.' Latin: 'Ergo quamvis de bonis et sanctis et aedificationum eloquiis perfectis discipulis propter taciturnitatis gravitatem rara loquendi concedatur licentia, quia scriptum est: In multiloquio non effugies peccatum.' Chapter 6 also says 'to speak and teach belongs to the master; to be silent and listen befits the disciple'. Chapter 42 opens 'Monks ought to cultivate silence at all times, but most of all in the hours of night' (Omni tempore silentium debent studere monachi). Chapter 4 lists 'Not to love much speaking' (Multum loqui non amare). The Gutenberg English (Doyle, 1948) is copyrighted and is not used.

stances.summary: The first step toward learning anything spiritual is to shut your mouth, listen to your elders, and try to live what you hear before you teach it.
stances.quote: For this is the first practical step towards learning, to receive the regulations and opinions of all the Elders with an earnest heart, and with lips that are dumb; and diligently to lay them up in your heart, and endeavour rather to perform than to teach them.
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Cassian (d. c. 435) puts this in the mouth of the Egyptian elder Nesteros, speaking to Cassian's friend Germanus and to Cassian ('especially you, John... enjoin absolute silence on your lips'); Cassian wrote the Conferences to hand on this teaching as his own programme. The Institutes praise the strict silence of Egyptian monks at prayer and at meals (Book 2 ch. 10; Book 4 ch. 17, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350704.htm). He is not naive about it: Institutes 12 describes a proud monk whose 'silence denotes not compunction or humility, but pride and wrath' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350712.htm).

stances.summary: I have seen many people fall into sin by talking, and hardly anyone by keeping quiet. Knowing how to be silent is harder than knowing how to speak. But silence must not be total or lazy: there is a time to speak.
stances.quote: How many have I seen to fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely one by keeping silent; and so it is more difficult to know how to keep silent than how to speak.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, NPNF Second Series vol. 10, 1896
stances.original: Quamplures vidi loquendo peccatum incidisse, vix quemquam tacendo: ideoque tacere nosse quam loqui difficilius est.
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis ministrorum)
stances.context: Written c. 388-391 for his clergy; he opens the whole work with silence, taking Psalm 39 ('I will take heed to my ways, that I offend not in my tongue') as his text. The very next chapter qualifies it: 'Ought we to be dumb? Certainly not. For: there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak... let us take care that we do not have to give it also for an idle silence' (1.3.9), and 'David rightly therefore enjoined on himself not constant silence, but watchfulness.' He also urges silence under insult (1.5.17-20 and 1.6.21). Latin from Latin Wikisource, De officiis ministrorum (https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/De_officiis_ministrorum).

stances.summary: People who talk too much scatter themselves and slide into gossip. But people who say too little are corrected too: bottled-up silence breeds pride and resentment, and failing to tell a neighbour his fault leaves the wound untreated. Curb the tongue, do not tie it up.
stances.quote: The tongue, therefore, should be discreetly curbed, not tied up fast.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF Second Series vol. 12, 1895
stances.location: Part 3, chapter 14 (Admonition 15: 'How the silent and the talkative are to be admonished')
stances.context: Written c. 590. The chapter gives both sides equal space. To the over-silent: 'often from bridling the tongue overmuch they suffer from more grievous loquacity in the heart'; 'For closed sores torment the more; since, when the corruption that is hot within is cast out, the pain is opened out for healing'; and those who see a neighbour's fault 'and yet refrain their tongue in silence... become the causers of death'. To the talkative: the mind 'scattered by much speaking' cannot return to itself, and 'every word is idle that lacks either a reason of just necessity or an intention of pious usefulness'. Part 2, chapter 4 says the ruler must be 'discreet in keeping silence, profitable in speech', because 'as incautious speaking leads into error, so indiscreet silence leaves in error those who might have been instructed', and calls timid pastors 'Dumb dogs, that cannot bark' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/36012.htm). His closed-sore line is the best patristic voice for the modern 'talk it out' pole.

stances.summary: Whether silence is good depends on the moment and the person. Beginners should keep silent so they can unlearn bad habits; the rash in speech need total silence until they are cured; but no one may keep silent when a brother sins.
stances.quote: Whether silence is good or not depends on the time and person, as we learn from inspired Scripture.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK), 1925
stances.location: Shorter Rule 208 (Rufinus's Latin numbering 136), 'Generally speaking is it good to practise silence?'
stances.context: Basil (d. 379) legislates for silence in the Longer Rules, question 13, 'That the practice of silence is beneficial for novices': silence 'induces forgetfulness of the past through lack of practice and affords leisure to learn good habits', so 'a novice must keep silence, except of course for the psalmody'. Shorter Rule 47 (Rufinus 122), 'Should we keep silence when men sin?', answers 'That we should not is clear from the commands of the Lord', and asks 'what shall we say of those who know and remain silent?' Letter 2 to Gregory of Nazianzus asks for a tongue 'purified from the gossip of the world' but also gives rules for good conversation: 'to be measured in speaking and hearing' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202002.htm). The djvu is OCR of the 1925 printing and has stray marginal letters.

stances.summary: He kept a whole Lent in total silence to master his tongue, and prized quiet. Yet when his wise old father fell silent, he begged him to speak: it is wrong for wisdom to be silent while inexperience talks.
stances.quote: I cannot allow the fountain to be dammed up, while the rivulet runs its course; the sun to be hidden, while the star shines forth; hoar hairs to be in retirement, while youth lays down the law; wisdom to be silent, while inexperience speaks with assurance.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF Second Series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 16, On His Father's Silence, Because of the Plague of Hail
stances.context: Oration 16 (c. 373) is addressed to his father, the bishop of Nazianzus, who had fallen silent after a hailstorm ruined the harvest. Section 4 asks him for 'words which are excellent rather than many', so even here he prefers few, weighty words. On the other side of his life: in Lent 382, after leaving Constantinople, he kept a complete fast from speech and wrote about it in Letters 107-119 and the poem 'On silence at the time of fasting' (Carmina II.1.34); the only English versions of these are modern and copyrighted (Storin 2019; Gilbert 2001), so they are not quoted, and this part rests on secondary sources. Letter 91 to Nectarius (NPNF vol. 7, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3103c.htm) has him 'valuing as we do the reward (which has no risk attaching to it) of silence, beyond everything'; the Greek there may mean quiet retirement rather than not speaking (not checked).

stances.summary: Not one idle word: idle talk slides into foul talk. Christians are soldiers in a war, and soldiers in a camp keep silence. But silence is wrong when a brother needs correcting.
stances.quote: Let there not be one idle word; for from idle words we fall also into foul words.
stances.translation: Gross Alexander, NPNF First Series vol. 13, 1889
stances.context: The homily is aimed at joking and banter more than at speech itself; he points to soldiers before battle: 'all is silence in the camps of those who are arrayed against each other.' Chrysostom (d. 407), the 'Golden Mouth', was a preacher, and he insists on speaking to correct others: to Titus, 'be not thou silent on that account. Do your part, although they may not receive you' (Homily 3 on Titus, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23083.htm), and to his people about blasphemers, 'Come forward and raise him up, both by words and by deeds' (Homilies on the Statues 1.33, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/190101.htm). So: against idle talk, for speech that corrects. Strength 1 because of that qualification.

stances.summary: Better to be a Christian and say nothing than to talk and not be one. A quiet bishop deserves more respect, and does more by his silence than empty talkers.
stances.quote: It is better for a man to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one. It is good to teach, if he who speaks also acts.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 107-110 on the way to martyrdom; this is the shorter (authentic) recension. The brackets are the translators'. He returns to silence often: 'the more any one sees the bishop keeping silence, the more ought he to revere him' (Ephesians 6), and he admires the bishop of Philadelphia 'who by his silence is able to accomplish more than those who vainly talk' (Philadelphians 1, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0108.htm). In the same chapter: 'He who possesses the word of Jesus, is truly able to hear even His very silence.' He also says 'love suffers me not to be silent in regard to you' (Ephesians 3), so he is not against speech; his theme is deeds over words.

stances.summary: At table and among friends, do not talk long or much, and never for show. Better to stay silent than to argue. Good speech belongs to the old and experienced.
stances.quote: For we ought not to speak long or much, nor ought we to speak frivolously.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.location: Book 2, chapter 7, 'Directions for those who live together'
stances.context: Clement (d. c. 215) writes etiquette for Christians at banquets. Same chapter: 'It is better to be silent than to contradict, and thereby add sin to ignorance', and 'silence is the excellence of women, and the safe prize of the young; but good speech is characteristic of experienced, mature age' (a line to handle with care; it is of its time). Chapter 6: 'Frivolous prating, too, is to be put to silence.' Measure rather than silence, so strength 1.

stances.summary: We are philosophers in deeds, not words. We do not talk about great things; we live them.
stances.quote: who are philosophers, not in words, but in deeds, and do not put forward our wisdom in our garb, but in truth— who are better acquainted with the consciousness, than with the boast, of virtues— who do not speak great things, but live them
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: On the Advantage of Patience (De bono patientiae), Treatise 9
stances.context: Written 256. This contrasts Christians with talkative pagan philosophers: words versus deeds, not speech versus silence as such, so it fits the claim only loosely (strength 1). The Latin 'non loquimur magna sed vivimus' borrows from Minucius Felix, Octavius 38, an earlier Christian writer. The same treatise praises Christ's 'most patient silence' before His accusers (section 23).

stances.summary: A good priest loves silence and privacy; the worldly cleric loves chatter in the streets and shops. Guard against a blabbing tongue and itching ears.
stances.quote: You love silence, meekness, privacy; he takes delight in talking and effrontery, in squares, and streets, and apothecaries' shops.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 394 to a young priest. Section 14: 'Beware also of a blabbing tongue and of itching ears.' Letter 125.15 (to the monk Rusticus, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001125.htm) says a monastery will teach 'one humility, another patience, a third silence'. But Letter 52.7 calls it 'a bad custom' that presbyters keep silent when bishops are present, so he wanted clergy to preach. Jerome was himself famously outspoken and a prolific, often furious letter writer; the reveal can enjoy that irony.

stances.summary: I tried keeping quiet so I would not sin with my tongue, and ended up holding back good words too. I came to regret the good I failed to say more than the wrong I said.
stances.quote: I began to be more grieved at having refrained from saying what I ought to have said, than I had before been grieved by having said what I ought not.
stances.translation: J. E. Tweed, NPNF First Series vol. 8, 1888
stances.context: Augustine expounds the psalmist's experience in the first person, as the path of a soul making progress; it is his reading, and he endorses it: 'Whilst afraid of saying any evil, I began to refrain from speaking what is good: and I condemned my determination; for I was holding my peace even from what is good.' He had first imposed silence on himself 'because I saw that everywhere speech was dangerous' after people 'cavilled at my words'. This is the exact reverse of Arsenius's saying, which makes a strong pairing. Confessions 1.4 adds: 'woe to those who keep silence, seeing that even they who say most are as the dumb' (about speaking of God, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/110101.htm). He was not against restraint: Possidius's Life (ch. 22) reports a verse on his dining table barring anyone who speaks ill of the absent (from general knowledge, not checked this session). Strength 1, because the passage targets fearful silence, not restraint as such.

stances.summary: There was a time for keeping quiet, but it is over. When truth is under attack the shepherds must cry out.
stances.quote: It is the time to speak, because the time for keeping silent is now past. Let Christ be looked for, because antichrist has prevailed. Let the shepherds cry out, because the hirelings have fled.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (no public-domain English of this work was found)
stances.original: Tempus est loquendi: quia jam praeteriit tempus tacendi. Christus exspectetur: quia obtinuit antichristus. Clament pastores: quia mercenarii fugerunt.
stances.context: Written c. 360-361 against the emperor Constantius II, who backed the Arian party. It is a call to speak out against error and power, not a view about everyday talk; Hilary grants that silence had its time. De Trinitate 1.37 gives his view of speech in general: 'I know, O Lord God Almighty, that I owe You, as the chief duty of my life, the devotion of all my words and thoughts to Yourself' (Watson and Pullan, NPNF Second Series vol. 9, 1899, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/330201.htm). Strength 1: disagreement on the grounds of courage, not of taste for talk.

stances.summary: A man who wanted to be thought a philosopher bore insults patiently for a while, then asked if people could see he was a philosopher now. The reply: I would have, if you had kept quiet.
stances.quote: cried out derisively: "_Now_, do you see that I am a philosopher?" The other, with biting sarcasm, retorted: "I should have hadst thou held thy peace."
stances.translation: H. R. James, The Consolation of Philosophy, 1897
stances.original: 'Iam tandem', inquit, 'intellegis me esse philosophum?' Tum ille nimium mordaciter: 'Intellexeram', inquit, 'si tacuisses'.
stances.context: Written c. 524 in prison. The story is told by Lady Philosophy, the book's voice of wisdom, against seeking praise; it is about vanity more than about silence, so strength 1. The underscores mark italics in the Gutenberg text. Latin from Latin Wikisource, De philosophiae consolatione, Liber Secundus (https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/De_philosophiae_consolatione/Liber_Secundus), checked through its search snippet only.

splits_fathers: Heavily one-sided toward agreement. Every monastic source (the desert sayings, Basil, Cassian, Benedict, Climacus, Isaac) and most bishops (Ignatius, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Jerome) say that talk is the usual road to sin and silence the usual road to God. Real voices on the other side exist, but none praise talk for its own sake. They defend speech when it corrects, teaches, confesses the truth or praises God. Augustine regrets the good he left unsaid when he went quiet out of fear. Hilary declares that 'the time for keeping silent is past'. Gregory the Great says the over-silent breed resentment and pride and let a neighbour's wound fester. Basil and Poemen make it depend on the time and the person. Gregory of Nazianzus practised a whole Lent of silence yet begged his father to break his. The most useful contrast for a reveal is Arsenius (never sorry for silence) against Augustine (more sorry for the good he left unsaid).
splits_people_today: Genuinely divided, which makes the claim useful. Many people, religious or not, agree with proverbs like 'listen more than you talk' and admire quiet people; introverts will tend to agree. Many others disagree: talking things through is widely seen as healthy, and 'bottling it up' as harmful (close to Gregory's closed sores). 'Speak your truth', 'silence is complicity' and the value placed on open communication in marriages and workplaces all push the other way, as does anyone who enjoys conversation and small talk as a way of loving people. Christians split too: contemplative and monastic traditions lean to silence, while evangelical and activist Christians stress speaking up, bearing witness and confronting wrong. A rough guess is a modest majority agreeing in the abstract, with a large and articulate minority disagreeing.

misattributions.line: I have often repented of having spoken, but never of having kept silent.
misattributions.truth: Arsenius did say it (Budge, Paradise vol. 2, Book I ch. 1 saying 53), but it is an older pagan proverb: Plutarch, On Talkativeness 23, credits it to the poet Simonides. Valerius Maximus is often cited as giving it to Xenocrates (not checked). The common wording is Benedicta Ward's copyrighted 1975 translation.

misattributions.line: Si tacuisses, philosophus mansisses (If you had kept silent, you would have remained a philosopher).
misattributions.truth: A later proverb built on Boethius. His text (Consolation 2, prose 7) reads 'Intellexeram, si tacuisses' ('I would have known it, had you kept silent'), spoken by a character in Lady Philosophy's story.

misattributions.line: Love silence above all things, because it brings you near to fruit that the tongue cannot express.
misattributions.truth: Genuine (Treatise 65 in Wensinck's 1923 translation). The circulating wording is from the copyrighted 1984 Holy Transfiguration Monastery translation. Use Wensinck: 'Love silence above all things. It brings thee near the fruit which the tongue is too weak to interpret.'

misattributions.line: O Lord and Master of my life, take from me the spirit of sloth, despair, lust of power, and idle talk.
misattributions.truth: The Lenten 'Prayer of St Ephrem' is a traditional attribution. It comes down in the Greek writings circulated under his name, not in his Syriac works, so it should not be used as proof of Ephrem's own view (not checked in a source this session; from general knowledge).

misattributions.line: There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Tempus tacendi et tempus loquendi).
misattributions.attributed_to: Hilary of Poitiers or Ambrose (in quotation lists)
misattributions.truth: This is Ecclesiastes 3:7. Ambrose and Gregory the Great quote it. Hilary's own line reverses it: 'Tempus est loquendi: quia jam praeteriit tempus tacendi' (Against Constantius 1).

notes: 1) For a quiz item, the claim works best if it pulls against the modern 'talk it out' and 'speak up' instincts, since almost every Father agrees with plain restraint. The disagree pole is thin and always qualified. Augustine (Psalm 39) and Gregory the Great (closed sores) are the strongest lines for it. Hilary is about courage, not chattiness. 2) Candidate reveal lines, all read in the source: Arsenius 'I have many times repented that I spoke, but that I held my peace I have never repented' against Augustine 'I began to be more grieved at having refrained from saying what I ought to have said'; Pambo 'If by my silence [we] are not helped, [we] shall not be builded by my word'; Ignatius 'better... to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one'; Gregory 'curbed, not tied up fast'. 3) Budge's page numbering: ecatholic2000 untitled-188 is Book I ch. 1 of the Sayings; untitled-195 is ch. 8; untitled-203 is the 'Questions and Answers on the Rule of Life'. Budge's square brackets are his own and are part of the text. 4) New Advent texts are NPNF/ANF translations lightly revised by Kevin Knight (for example 'You' for 'Thee'); quote the page as it stands. 5) Searched with no usable result: Syncletica (no saying on speech in Budge), Macrina and Gregory of Nyssa, Tertullian, Justin, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Novatian, Perpetua, Lactantius, Athanasius as author, Martin of Tours, Paulinus of Nola, Pelagius. Pelagius's Letter to Demetrias might have something but only Latin or modern English exist, and it was not checked. 6) Capitals for God: Climacus's own rendering uses 'Him'; the other quotations already capitalise or have no pronoun for God.
